c1-control-r6.card:
id: r6-s-ldef-nc-disp
parents:

operation: specialisation
language: cuda_cpp
niche:
  mem: ldg256
  st: direct
  grid: oneshot
  launch: fused
  tile: rows16
  red: halfwarp
  cache: stream
  spec: dispatch:size
hypothesis: >-
  My estimate of what the parent's ~3.2 us fixed cost on small inputs is made of:
  (a) CUPTI launch-to-end span of a near-empty kernel, about 1-1.5 us;
  (b) loaded DRAM latency plus TLB misses on first touch of fresh pool addresses, about 1 us;
  (c) store drain and grid exit, about 0.3-0.5 us;
  (d) possibly extra DRAM write-backs: every line we allocate in an L2 full of the flush's dirty zero lines
  may evict one of them.
  (a)-(c) are mostly outside a kernel's control. r4-cute-ldg256-sw2-disp tests warp and CTA dispatch.
  This candidate tests (d) only. For B*S <= 600, x loads carry L2 evict_first and weights use ld.global.nc,
  the load policy CAKE kept after paired cold-L2 B200 tests. Allocations for input lines then recycle our
  own clean lines instead of evicting dirty flush lines, and output stores (still evict_last) can take the
  place of those clean input lines. Larger sizes run the parent unchanged, so the B200 result isolates the
  effect on S.
  Measured on A100 (128-bit fallback), against the parent: S +0.3% (noise; -2.2%, -1.1% at 25 MB, +1.5 to +1.8%
  at 12.6 MB), M/L 0%. The near-peak marginal bandwidth on both GPUs already argues that (d) is small. So
  this is mainly a cheap B200 check of the mechanism: an expected gain of 0 to 3% on S, B200-only if it
  appears at all.
  Also tried and rejected: 2-4 tiles per CTA. On A100 that was -6% at 128 tokens and +14% at 256 tokens. The
  128-token gain is an A100 wave effect (the parent runs 1.8 waves on 108 SMs, but one wave on B200's 148).
  It duplicates r4-cute, and the 2-tile kernel needs 48 registers on sm_100a, so 5 CTAs/SM would spill
  256 tokens into a second wave.
expected_effect:
  S:
    pct: -1.5
    confidence: low
  M:
    pct: 0
    confidence: high
  L:
    pct: 0
    confidence: high
resources_sm100a:
  regs_per_thread: 31
  smem_per_cta_bytes: 0
  threads_per_cta: 256
  ctas_per_sm: 8
  bytes_in_flight_per_sm: 65536
  launches_per_call: 1
knobs:
  ROWS: 16
  THREADS: 256
  S_MAX_TOKENS: 600
  S_load_policy: "x: L2::cache_hint 0x12F0000000000000 (evict_first); w: ld.global.nc"
  store_policy: "L2 evict_last, fraction 1.0 (all sizes)"
dispatch:
  - max_tokens: 600
    kernel: qk_rms_kernel<true>
    meta:
      ROWS: 16
      THREADS: 256
      loads: "x evict_first, w nc"
  - max_tokens: 1000000000
    kernel: qk_rms_kernel<false>
    meta:
      ROWS: 16
      THREADS: 256
      note: "identical to parent r5-ldg256-os-r16-stel"
runs_on:
  H200:
    runs: true
    representative: false
    note: "128-bit fallback; the L2 is 50 MB instead of 126 MB, so the dirty-flush interaction differs"
  A100:
    runs: true
    representative: false
    note: "measured S +0.3%, M 0.0%, L -0.1% vs parent (noise); 16/16 pass"
  L40S:
    runs: true
    representative: false
risks:
  - "Term (d) may be negligible on B200, since marginal bandwidth between 12.6 and 25 MB is already about 7.9 TB/s. The expected result is then about 0 on S."
  - "On A100, evict_first loads hurt L by 4% (r5 session). That is why they apply only to B*S <= 600; the 586-token workload (57.6 MB) is the one most exposed if B200 behaves the same way."
  - "S-band noise on the portal is about 5%, so one submission cannot resolve an effect of 1-3%."
measure_first:
  - H200
compliance:
  single_stream: true
  no_cross_call_state: true
  fp32_math: true
  no_threads_or_fork: true
  no_precompiled_binaries: true

r1-bulk1d-ring-r16s16.card:

  cache: stream

  v039 serialises load, reduce and store inside each persistent program and never prefetches, so its outstanding
  reads per SM fall well below the ~43-64 KB B200 needs. A dedicated producer thread keeps 16 x 8 KB cp.async.bulk
  loads in flight per SM. Consumer warps release stages right after their reduction. Weights sit in shared memory.
  Read issue is therefore decoupled from compute latency at one instruction per 8 KB, which should lift
  sustained bandwidth from 5.8 to about 7 TB/s.

  S:
    pct: -5
    confidence: low
  M:
    pct: -12
    confidence: low
  L:
    pct: -17
    confidence: medium

  regs_per_thread: 32
  smem_per_cta_bytes: 180488
  threads_per_cta: 544
  ctas_per_sm: 1
  bytes_in_flight_per_sm: 131072
  launches_per_call: 1
knobs:
  TR: 16
  STAGES: 16
  consumer_warps: 16
  producer_warps: 1
  grid: num_SMs
runs_on:
  H200:
    runs: true
    representative: true
    note: "same bulk/mbarrier path (sm_90); H200 needs less in flight, so expect it to show correctness and a moderate gain, not the full B200 gain"
  A100:
    runs: true
    representative: false
    note: "runs the plain warp-per-row fallback (no cp.async.bulk on sm_80); correctness only"
  L40S:
    runs: true
    representative: false
    note: "fallback path; correctness only"
risks:
  - "One CTA per SM with 16 consumer warps: if per-tile consumer latency (wait, LDS, 5 shuffles, rsqrt, STG) exceeds about 520 clk at 1.5 GHz, the consumers become the bottleneck; then try 2 rows per warp with TR=32 or 8 KB tiles over 2 CTAs/SM."
  - "Direct stores from only 16 warps per SM may cap write throughput; st:bulk via smem staging is the follow-up axis."
  - "A single producer thread issues all bulk copies; issue rate is about 1 per 520 clk needed, so it should be fine, but it is unmeasured on B200."
  - "Prologue (mbarrier init and 48 KB weight bulk load, an L2 hit after the first CTA) adds to S-band fixed cost; S-band loads are all issued up front, which may offset it."
  - "180 KB of dynamic smem needs the cudaFuncSetAttribute opt-in (done once on the host); it compiles for sm_100a only via the inline-PTX paths guarded by __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900."
measure_first:
  - H200
compliance:
  single_stream: true
  no_cross_call_state: true
  fp32_math: true
  no_threads_or_fork: true

r10-bulk1d-ring-stel.card:
id: r10-bulk1d-ring-stel
parents:
  - r6-s-ldef-nc-disp
operation: new_design
language: cuda_cpp
niche:
  mem: bulk1d
  st: direct
  grid: persistent
  launch: fused
  tile: rows16
  red: halfwarp
  cache: stream
  spec: all
hypothesis: >-
  Exploration of explore:bulk-pipeline. Hypothesis: a 1-D TMA ring (cp.async.bulk + mbarrier) moves bytes with
  fewer SM instructions, which the portal's 1500 MHz SM clock should reward. Refuted on the rented B200.
  The TMA bulk-store path is about 27% slower than STG.256 for a write-only stream. Bulk loads are about 3% slower
  than LDG.256 at 805 MB and add about 0.3-0.4 us of fixed cost. A persistent ring also adds about 0.8 us of
  per-CTA serialisation at small sizes. The best variant uses bulk loads, a 4 x 8 KB ring, and STG.256 stores with
  evict_last. It passes 16/16 but is slower than r6 in every band: rented S +18.8%, M +7.1%, L +1.6%;
  predicted portal score 0.58. The LDG kernel already runs at plain-copy speed, so there are no SM cycles for TMA
  to save.
expected_effect:
  S:
    pct: 17
    confidence: high
  M:
    pct: 7
    confidence: medium
  L:
    pct: 2
    confidence: medium
resources_sm100a:
  regs_per_thread: 32
  smem_per_cta_bytes: 33824
  threads_per_cta: 256
  ctas_per_sm: 4
  bytes_in_flight_per_sm: 131072
  launches_per_call: 1
knobs:
  ROWS: 16
  STAGES: 4
  THREADS: 256
  CTAS_PER_SM: "4 if tokens <= 2048 else 2"
  tile_order: strided (tile = blockIdx + j*grid)
  store: "st.global.v8 L2::cache_hint evict_last"
findings:
  - "probe: pure TMA copy (bulk load -> bulk store, single-thread CTAs, contiguous chunks 4-32 KB) vs LDG.256/STG.256 copy: 12.6 MB 4.4 vs 3.9 us, 25 MB 5.7 vs 5.25, 101 MB 14.8-16.4 vs 14.1, 805 MB 126-131 vs 116 [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: loads only, bulk vs LDG.256: 805 MB 74.9 vs 72.6 us (+3%), 101 MB 12.4 vs 11.7, 12.6 MB 4.00 vs 3.68 [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: stores only, bulk store (evict_last hint) vs STG.256 evict_last: 805 MB 69.1 vs 54.6 us (+27%), 101 MB 8.6 vs 7.5, 12.6 MB 2.55 vs 2.18. Bulk stores are the main bottleneck of a full-TMA pipeline [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: bulk stores without the L2 hint are slower still (101 MB copy 18.6 vs 15.0 us with evict_last) [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: rmsnorm ring with bulk stores (in-place smem write-back) is 5-40% slower than with direct STG stores at every size [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: more bytes in flight hurts the ring at 805 MB: S4 strided x2 CTAs/SM 117.3 us; x3 127; x4 131; S8/S12 124-134; contiguous per-CTA ranges are no better than strided. base LDG kernel 115.7 [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: at 12.6 MB even a ring that issues all loads up front (r8, S6, 8 CTAs/SM, 1-2 tiles per CTA) is 4.83 us vs 4.04 for one-shot LDG.256; TMA plus mbarrier setup adds about 0.8 us [probe_b200]"
  - "run_tests: this kernel 16/16 pass; rented B200 vs r6: S +18.8%, M +7.1%, L +1.6%; predicted portal 0.5815 +- 0.012 [run_tests]"
  - "dead end: bulk/TMA paths for #38 on B200; the one-shot LDG.256/STG.256 kernel already runs at plain-copy speed, so there is no SM work for TMA to save. Do not revisit unless a new store mechanism appears"
  - "tooling: b200probe harness_time sometimes reports 'No timing results' on its first call in a process; retry once [probe_b200]"
paths:
  - max_tokens: 2048
    lang: cuda
    width: 256
    threads: 256
    rows: 16
    grid: persistent
    mem: tma
    w: nc
    st: el
  - max_tokens: null
    lang: cuda
    width: 256
    threads: 256
    rows: 16
    grid: persistent
    mem: tma
    w: nc
    st: el
runs_on:
  H200:
    runs: true
    representative: false
    note: "bulk copies run on sm_90, but stores fall back to 128-bit and the L2 is smaller"
  A100:
    runs: false
    representative: false
    note: "no cp.async.bulk / mbarrier tx on sm_80"
  L40S:
    runs: false
    representative: false
risks:
  - "Slower than the current best in every band; do not submit for score. It exists as the bulk1d niche record."
  - "The portal's lower SM clock could narrow the gap slightly at L, but the bulk-load path itself is slower than LDG even in a loads-only test"
measure_first:
  - B200
compliance:
  single_stream: true
  no_cross_call_state: true
  fp32_math: true
  no_threads_or_fork: true
  no_precompiled_binaries: true

task.instructions: A hand-written bulk-copy pipeline in CUDA C++: cp.async.bulk (1-D TMA) global to shared memory with mbarrier completion, normalise from shared memory, then store (cp.async.bulk shared to global, or st.global with evict_last), double or triple buffered in a persistent single wave. The aim is fewer SM instructions per byte, which the portal's 1500 MHz SM clock rewards. Earlier Triton TMA designs (g2-tma, g2-tmaws) were slow for other reasons; this is a different bet. First probe a bulk-copy pipeline copy against a plain LDG/STG copy at 12.6, 101 and 805 MB. This is an EXPLORATION task: the goal is to learn whether this idea can move some size band by 3% or more on the portal, not to edge out the current best by 0.1%. You may discard the parent's design entirely; it is given for reference. Test the idea's core assumption with probe_b200 first (seconds per probe). If the idea does not pan out, still return your best version of it as the candidate and record what you learned in the card's findings: negative results are valuable and go into the lab notebook for later rounds. Keep the kernel copy-like (memory-bound): the portal locks the SM clock lower than the test bench and penalises extra SM work per byte (problem card section 7). CUDA C++ uses the two-file layout.

  B*S <= 600 to B*S <= 1024, plain loads above. Measured on the rented B200 vs r6: S -0.8%, M -1.2%,
  L +0.3% (noise). The predicted portal score is 0.611 +- 0.009.

    confidence: medium
  M:
    pct: -1
    confidence: low
  L:
    pct: 0
    confidence: high
resources_sm100a:

findings:
  - "probe: under harness timing, evict_last stores (createpolicy) beat plain stores by 8% at 128 tokens, 12% at 256, 14% at 586, 19% at 1024, 12% at 2048, 5% at 4096 and 2.5% at 8192 tokens; r5's mechanism reproduces on the rented B200 [probe_b200]"
  - "dead end: evict_last on only the last 48/80/112 MB of output blocks (earlier stores evict_normal or evict_first) is within +-1% of all-evict_last at 2048-8192 tokens; fractional evict_last 0.5/0.75 is the same or up to 5% worse (0.5 at 1024 tokens). The store-side end state is at its limit [probe_b200]"
  - "dead end: block order (reversed, K first, Q/K interleaved) is within 1% at 128-256 tokens, so the harness's input copies leave no useful L2 residency; the 586-8192 token sizes were not measured because a harness_time CUPTI error ended the run [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: the dirty zero-fill flush costs reads, not writes. Event timing after a zero_ flush vs a zero_+read flush: read-only kernels +7..11 us at 100-400 MB, copy +5..6 us, write-only +-1 us [probe_b200]"
  - "probe: read-only 100/400 MB under harness timing: plain/.nc/.cs/.lu/L1::no_allocate/L2::evict_last 21.9/75.4 us; ld.global.L2::evict_first or createpolicy evict_first 18.6/65-66 us (-15%/-13%); createpolicy evict_unchanged no gain [probe_b200]"
  - "caveat: the CUTLASS EVICT_FIRST constant 0x12F0000000000000 was a no-op when passed as a kernel argument (read-only and full kernel), but works like the qualifier when written into the instruction as an immediate (r6's form). r6's S-band evict_first was therefore real. Cause unknown; prefer the qualifier or createpolicy [probe_b200]"

  - "result: run_tests vs r6: S -0.8%, M -1.2% (1024 tokens -1.7..-2.4%), L +0.3%; predicted portal 0.6112 +- 0.0088 [run_tests]"
  - "open: evict_last saves only 3-4 us (about 25-30 MB of write-back) at every size from 1024 to 8192 tokens, not the 126 MB L2; the rest of L2 may be held by the harness's dirty lines or capped for evict_last.
